Citation:

```{r}
library(RTextTools)
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

data(NYTimes)

NYTimes_US <- NYTimes |>
    select(Article_ID, Title) |>
    filter(str_detect(Title, "\\bU.S\\b", negate = FALSE)) |>
    mutate(word_list = str_to_lower(str_extract(Title, "(?<=\\bU.S\\b. )\\w+"))) |>
    group_by(word_list) |> 
    filter(!is.na(word_list)) |>
    summarize(count = n()) |>
    arrange(desc(count)) |>
    mutate(word_list = fct_reorder(word_list, count, .desc = TRUE)) |>
    head(30)

NYTimes_US |>
    ggplot(aes (x = word_list, y = count)) + 
    geom_col() +
    labs(
        title = "Top 30 words following “U.S.” in NYT article headlines (1996-2006)",
        x="",
        y="Count"
    ) +
    theme(axis.text.x=element_text(angle = -45, hjust = 0))  
```

Description: This column graph displays the top 30 words across all NYT article headlines 
(reported in this dataset) from 1996-2006. The word with the greatest frequency is "is": 16. Followed by
"to", 10, and "and", 7. I'm particulary interested in the preceding words "troops" and "appeals" showing up 7 times;
this may suggest some correlation between U.S. media and war; violence; politics. 

```{r}
NYTimes_Month <- NYTimes |>
    select(Date, Title) |>
    mutate(Date = as.integer(year(dmy(Date)))) |>
    mutate(word_list = str_extract(Title, "(?i)\\bkill|war|violence")) |>
    select(Date, word_list) |>
    filter(!is.na(word_list)) |>
    group_by(Date) |>
    summarize(Count = n()) 

NYTimes_Month |> 
    ggplot(aes(x=Date, y=Count)) +
    geom_line() + 
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1996, 2006, by = 1)) +
    annotate("text", x = 2003, y = 49, label = "U.S. invades Iraq", vjust = -.25) +
    annotate("point", x = 2003, y =49) + 
    labs(
        title = "Occurrence of 'kill'; 'war'; 'violence' in NYT headlines (1996-2006)",
        x = "",
        y = "Count"
    )
```

Description: This line graph displays the occurence of 'kill'; 'war'; and 'violence' across NYT headlines from 1996-2006. The trio of words
appeared most often in NYT headlines in 2003, 49 times (concurrent to U.S. invasion of Iraq). They appear least frequent in 1998 and 2005, they tie for 10 times; 
I am not sure what global-historical correlation these two years lower values represents. It is interesting to note the upward trend in these trio words
reported in NYT headlines following 2001 (the year 9/11 occured): the U.S.'s descent into global affair/war.
